ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A spherical cloud of sparse interstellar gas, initially at rest with radius $r_0$ and mass $m$, collapses due to its own gravity. The initial temperature of the gas and its surroundings is uniformly $T_0$. The gas is assumed to be ideal with average molar mass $\mu$ and adiabatic index $\gamma > \frac{4}{3}$. It is assumed that $G \frac{m \mu}{r_0} \gg R T_0$, where $R$ is the gas constant and $G$ is the gravitational constant.

1. i. During much of the collapse, the gas is so transparent that any heat generated is immediately radiated away, i.e. the ball stays in thermodynamic equilibrium with its surroundings. What is the number of times, $n$, by which the pressure increases when the radius is halved to $r_{1}=0.5 r_{0}$? Assume that the gas density remains uniform.
2. ii. Estimate the time $t_{2}$ needed for the radius to shrink from $r_{0}$ to $r_{2}=0.95 r_{0}$. Neglect the change of the gravity field at the position of a falling gas particle.
3. iii. Assuming that the pressure remains negligible, find the time $t_{r \rightarrow 0}$ needed for the ball to collapse from $r_{0}$ down to a much smaller radius, using Kepler's Laws.
4. iv. At some radius $r_{3} \ll r_{0}$, the gas becomes dense enough to be opaque to the heat radiation. Calculate the amount of heat $Q$ radiated away during the collapse from the radius $r_{0}$ down to $r_{3}$.
5. v. For radii smaller than $r_{3}$ you may neglect heat loss due to radiation. Determine how the temperature $T$ of the ball depends on its radius for $r<r_{3}$.
6. vi. Eventually we cannot neglect the effect of the pressure on the dynamics of the gas and the collapse stops at $r=r_{4}$ (with $r_{4} \ll r_{3}$). However, the radiation loss can still be neglected and the temperature is not yet high enough to ignite nuclear fusion. The pressure of such a protostar is not uniform anymore, but rough estimates with inaccurate numerical prefactors can still be done. Estimate the final radius $r_{4}$ and the respective temperature $T_{4}$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$n=8$
$t_2 \approx \sqrt{\frac{0.1 r_{0}^{3}}{G m}}$
$t_{r \rightarrow 0}=\pi \sqrt{\frac{r_{0}^{3}}{8 G m}}$
$Q=\frac{3 m R T_{0}}{\mu} \ln \frac{r_{0}}{r_{3}}$
$T(r)=T_{0}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r}\right)^{3 \gamma-3}$
$r_{4} = r_{3}\left(\frac{R T_{0} r_{3}}{\mu m G}\right)^{\frac{1}{3 \gamma-4}}$, $T_{4} \approx T_{0}\left(\frac{R T_{0} r_{3}}{\mu m G}\right)^{\frac{3 \gamma-3}{4-3 \gamma}}$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: No image evidence is needed; the problem is fully specified in text. The cloud has mass m, initial radius r0, initial temperature T0, ideal-gas molar mass μ, and γ > 4/3. (i) In the transparent stage the gas remains in thermal equilibrium with the surroundings, so T = T0. For an ideal gas, pV = (m/μ)RT0, hence p ∝ 1/V. With uniform density, V ∝ r^3. Halving the radius gives V1 = V0/8, so p1/p0 = 8. (ii) For the radius to shrink from r0 to 0.95r0, the surface falls a distance Δr = 0.05r0. Neglecting the change in the gravity field, take g ≈ Gm/r0^2. Starting from rest, Δr = gt2^2/2, so t2 = sqrt(2Δr/g) = sqrt(0.1r0^3/(Gm)). (iii) With pressure negligible, the surface particle moves as if released from rest at apocenter r0 in a degenerate Kepler ellipse around mass m. The semimajor axis is a = r0/2. The orbital period is 2π sqrt(a^3/(Gm)), and the fall to r ≈ 0 is half a period. Therefore t_{r→0} = π sqrt(a^3/(Gm)) = π sqrt(r0^3/(8Gm)). (iv) During transparent contraction the process is isothermal, so for an ideal gas ΔU = 0. The heat radiated equals the work done on the gas: Q = ∫ from V0 to V3 of -p dV. Since p = (m/μ)RT0/V, Q = (mRT0/μ) ln(V0/V3). Because V ∝ r^3, ln(V0/V3) = 3 ln(r0/r3), so Q = (3mRT0/μ) ln(r0/r3). (v) For r < r3, radiation loss is neglected, so the contraction is adiabatic. Thus TV^{γ-1} = constant. Since V ∝ r^3 and T(r3) = T0, T(r) = T0(r3/r)^{3γ-3}. (vi) The collapse stops when thermal pressure effects become comparable to gravity. For an order-of-magnitude estimate, set RT4/μ ≈ Gm/r4. Also T4 = T0(r3/r4)^{3γ-3}. Combining gives (RT0/μ)(r3/r4)^{3γ-3} ≈ Gm/r4, hence r4^{3γ-4} ≈ (RT0/(μGm))r3^{3γ-3}. Therefore r4 = r3(RT0 r3/(μmG))^{1/(3γ-4)}. Substituting this into the adiabatic temperature law gives T4 ≈ T0(RT0 r3/(μmG))^{(3γ-3)/(4-3γ)}.
